## Chapter Summary

Monitoring runs audit tests every period on new data and keeps the results over time. Continuous auditing is internal audit's ongoing, technology-based assessment of risks and controls; continuous monitoring is management's ongoing review of its own controls, on which continuous auditing depends. Rule tests produce exceptions, records that fail a deterministic rule, while analytical tests produce anomalies, records or periods that differ from what is expected and call for a closer look. A monitoring system must keep its exceptions reviewable, through tests that state their rule, population, frequency, and expected result, and its results belong to the people who oversee the controls rather than to the people whose transactions it tests.

An exception register holds the exceptions of every test in one table, one row per exception per test, with the same columns whatever the process. In Power BI it is built in Power Query: each test becomes a flag column, unpivoting turns the flags into rows from which the exceptions are kept, and appending stacks the exceptions of several processes, the counterpart of Chapter 12's UNION ALL, matching columns by name rather than position. Tutorial 16.1 rebuilt Chapter 8's journal entry tests and risk scores, drilled from the highest-scoring entry to its ledger lines, and reconciled the population of entries to the ledger. Tutorial 16.2 added Chapter 12's purchasing and payroll tests, appended the register, and measured each test's exceptions against its population.

The monitoring page shows exceptions by test and month as a heat map, with the number in every cell, and leads by drill-through to the documents behind a cell. Charles River's register showed two patterns: most exceptions cluster in the first month of every year, which points to how the controls operate at that time, and one test, registers approved by the employee they pay, recurs every month, which points to the design of the control. Counting exceptions by approver brought back the concentration of approval that Chapter 12 found.

Row-level security restricts the rows each user can see through roles of DAX rules. A rule filters its table and, through active relationships, the tables related to it, so rules belong on dimensions, and tables no relationship reaches stay unfiltered. A dynamic role compares USERPRINCIPALNAME with a security table, roles are additive, and editors of a workspace bypass the rules. Row-level security cannot hide columns, which object-level security does, or pages, which simply show the rows a viewer may see. Tutorial 16.3 found that Charles River's managers of record name terminated employees and omit the actual managers, built a security table approved by the controller and a role that denies anyone missing from it, and tested the role with View as, finding pages that become silently partial.

A report reaches its readers by being published to a workspace in the Power BI service. Sharing requires a Pro or Premium Per User license, or a capacity for free readers; managers should be workspace Viewers or app readers so that the rules apply to them; app audiences show different reports to different groups; a local source needs a gateway for scheduled refresh; Publish to web makes a report public and must never be used for confidential data; and sensitivity labels and export settings govern what happens when data leaves the report.
